bib.title: Chapter 16: Applications and Case Studies, in Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.)

question: How have RL methods been applied to real problems, and what role do domain knowledge, representation and search play in each case?
contributions: Eight case studies: TD-Gammon, Samuel's checkers, Watson DD wagering, RL DRAM memory control, DQN on Atari, AlphaGo and AlphaGo Zero, personalised web services (Adobe LTV), thermal soaring

results.claim: TD-Gammon 0.0 (raw 198-unit board encoding, no backgammon features) matched the best earlier programs after about 300,000 self-play games.
results.setup: TD(lambda) + backprop ANN, 40 hidden units, self-play, afterstate move selection, update after every move
results.quote: After playing about 300,000 games against itself

results.claim: The TD-Gammon network input is 198 units.
results.setup: Tesauro's 0.0 representation: 4 units x 2 colours x 24 points + 2 bar + 2 borne-off + 2 turn
results.quote: There were a total of 198 input units to the network.

results.claim: Backgammon game tree has an effective branching factor of about 400, too large for conventional heuristic search.
results.setup: backgammon, about 20 ways to play a typical roll times opponent dice rolls

results.claim: TD-Gammon 3.0 (80 hidden units, 1,500,000 training games) beat Kazaros by 6 points over 20 games.
results.setup: Tesauro's 1990s human matches; point margins from the program's side, negative = loss
results.note: TD-Gammon 3.0/3.1 used 160 hidden units and 3-ply search per text, but Table 16.1 lists 80 hidden units for 3.0

results.claim: Trajectory sampling instead of full-width search cut TD-Gammon's live error rate 4x-6x at about 5-10 s per move.
results.setup: follow-on to TD-Gammon, Tesauro and Galperin (1997)

results.claim: Samuel's self-play generalisation learner could get worse with experience because it had no reward or terminal grounding; Samuel had to reset the largest-magnitude weight to zero.
results.setup: Samuel checkers 1959; value function a linear scoring polynomial with a fixed-weight piece-advantage feature
results.quote: it should have been possible for it to become worse with experience

results.claim: Watson's simulated win rate with a baseline heuristic Daily-Double wagering strategy was 61%.
results.source: Tesauro, Gondek, Lechner, Fan, and Prager (2012, 2013)
results.setup: Simulation vs. human-opponent models (Average, Champion, Grand Champion), DD wagering only

results.claim: Learned state values with a default confidence raised Watson's simulated win rate to 64%.
results.setup: same simulation setup

results.claim: Adding live in-category confidence raised Watson's simulated win rate to 67%, though DD wagering occurs only about 1.5 to 2 times per game.
results.setup: same simulation setup

results.claim: Watson's wagering value function was learned from simulated games against opponent models built from a fan archive of nearly 300,000 clues, not from self-play.
results.setup: Three models: Average Contestant (all data), Champion (100 best players), Grand Champion (10 best)

results.claim: Risk-neutral argmax over action values 'incurred a frightening amount of risk', so Watson subtracted a fraction of the std. dev. of the correct/incorrect afterstate values and barred bets that drop the wrong-answer value below a limit.
results.setup: Watson DD wagering, q(s,bet)=pDD v(SW+bet)+(1-pDD) v(SW-bet)

results.setup: Simulation, 4GHz 4-core chip, nine memory-intensive parallel scientific and data-mining workloads, performance = inverse execution time normalised to FR-FCFS
results.quote: by from 7% to 33% over the nine applications

results.setup: same

results.claim: The RL controller closed 27% of the gap to the unrealisable Optimistic controller.
results.setup: same

results.claim: Online-learning controller was 8% better than the same controller with action values frozen after training on all nine benchmarks.
results.setup: same; fixed policy trained on all nine benchmarks

results.claim: Memory controller learner: Sarsa, tile coding with 32 tilings of 256 16-bit action values, epsilon-greedy 0.05, six integer state features, reward 1 on read/write else 0; action constraint sets A(St) keep exploration inside hardware-safe region.

results.claim: DQN trained 50 million frames per game (about 38 days of experience), from random weights per game, evaluated as mean over 30 sessions of up to 5 minutes.
results.setup: 49 Atari 2600 games, single architecture and hyperparameters for all
results.quote: 50 million frames, which corresponds to about 38 days

results.claim: DQN beat the best previous RL system on all but 6 games and the professional human tester on 22 games.
results.setup: Atari, professional tester after 2 hours practice, about 20 episodes of up to 5 minutes per game
results.quote: played better than the human player on 22 of the games

results.claim: DQN reached or exceeded human level (>=75% of human score) on 29 of 46 games.
results.setup: Atari threshold of 75% of the human score
results.quote: reached or exceeded human level on 29 of the 46 games

results.claim: DQN input is 84x84x4 (four stacked luminance frames) from 210x160 frames.
results.setup: Atari preprocessing, identical across games

results.claim: DQN network: conv 32 20x20, 64 9x9, 64 7x7 maps, 3,136 units into 512 fully connected, 18 outputs.
results.setup: ReLU units; 4 to 18 valid actions per game

results.claim: DQN used mini-batches of 32, RMSProp, replay memory, a target network refreshed every C updates, TD error clipped to [-1,1], reward clipped to +1/-1/0, epsilon decayed linearly over the first million frames.
results.setup: values from informal search on a small set of games, then fixed

results.claim: Experience replay and the duplicate target network each improved DQN significantly and dramatically together; the deep conv net beat a single linear layer on all 5 test games.

results.claim: Contextual bandit news personalisation improved click-through rate by 12.5% over a standard non-associative bandit.

limits: Case-study summaries of other groups' work; all numbers are reported, none measured by the authors.
Samuel's learner lacked reward grounding and could degrade; the text says a constant value function would satisfy it.
DQN fell short on games needing deep planning (Montezuma's Revenge about random); one network per game, not one agent for all games.
Memory controller was only simulated, never fabricated.
Watson self-play was rejected: imperfect information and Watson unlike any human contestant.
Chapter says applications 'typically require as much art as science'.
Hyperparameters such as DQN's replay size, C, learning rate and gamma are not given here.
practices: Incorporate domain knowledge through features, constraints and opponent models, and note where it enters (chapter intro, p.421).
Represent the state with a small number of conceptually distinct, similarly scaled inputs (TD-Gammon encoding, s16.1).
Combine learned value functions with decision-time search (TD-Gammon 2-3 ply; AlphaGo MCTS) (s16.1, s16.6).
Fix a reward that ties the value function to the true outcome; self-consistency alone can collapse (s16.2).
Limit exploration with pre-defined legal-action sets so learning cannot violate hardware constraints (s16.4).
Standardise rewards (clip to +1/-1/0) and clip TD error to [-1,1] so one step size works across tasks (s16.5).
Use experience replay and a periodically frozen target network to stabilise bootstrapped Q-learning with function approximation (s16.5).
Initialise RL from supervised learning on expert data when available (AlphaGo), or use pure self-play with search as policy improvement (AlphaGo Zero) (s16.6).
Subtract a variance penalty and bound the downside when maximising expected value in high-stakes decisions (Watson, s16.3).
Use off-policy evaluation with high-confidence guarantees before deploying a new policy (s16.7).
Shape rewards experimentally when the natural terminal reward is too sparse (thermal soaring, s16.8).
